summary: The note explains how small and medium enterprises (SMEs) use blockchain's distributed ledger to improve transparency and security, using case examples across supply chains, payments, fraud prevention, and client services. It also covers challenges such as scalability, integration costs, and energy use, and describes education and collaboration efforts that lower adoption barriers. It concludes that SMEs that adopt blockchain wisely and sustainably stand to gain the most.
one_line: Case studies show SMEs using blockchain for supply chain transparency, payments, fraud prevention and client trust, despite scalability, cost and energy challenges.
key_facts: Blockchain's distributed ledger stores transactional records in multiple locations, updated in real time, making them nearly impossible to alter once recorded.

In October 2023, Veronica Lee, CEO of apparel manufacturer Veronica's Vogue Ventures, integrated blockchain into supply chain management to track products from raw material to final sale, which reduced product counterfeiting.

In December 2023, bespoke furniture maker Oak & Maple Ltd. integrated blockchain into invoicing and payments; CFO Michael Rodriguez said traditional payment methods created bottlenecks and security concerns.
Oak & Maple Ltd.'s auditable transaction history helped it more readily secure loans for business expansion by lowering perceived lender risk.
In February 2024, cybersecurity SME SecureTech Innovations built a tamper-proof record-keeping service on blockchain; CTO Dr. Adrian Wu said data cannot be altered without detection.
SecureTech's clients, mainly other SMEs, use the service to keep records of intellectual property, contractual agreements, and customer data.
Blockchain challenges for SMEs include scalability, resources needed to integrate with existing systems, and energy consumption.

In May 2024, GreenFuture Insights advised an SME consortium on offsetting blockchain's carbon footprint through renewable energy and carbon credits; CEO Helena Byrne said benefits must be weighed against environmental impact.

In August 2024, tech entrepreneurs led by Jaxon Smythe of InnovateNow launched a collaborative initiative offering workshops, resources, and a blockchain-as-a-service platform so SMEs can adopt blockchain without in-house expertise.
In September 2024, family-run law firm Litwell Legal launched a blockchain-based platform letting clients monitor the progress of their legal documents in real time.
Founding partner Elizabeth Litwell said the transparency affirmed Litwell Legal's commitment to accountability and significantly improved client satisfaction rates.
The note says SMEs have been observed harnessing blockchain to bolster operational integrity since September 2023.
